title: Why Is Christmas on December 25?
subtitle: A Roman book of 354, a feast of the Unconquered on the same day, a count from March 25, and what the oldest sources can and cannot tell us

sources.title: Luke 2:4-20 and Matthew 2:1-12 (Erasmus, Novum Testamentum omne, Basel [1520], UB Basel UBH BibG C 394, p.155); A. McGowan on the absence of early annual birth feasts
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 1): no day or month in the Gospels; no clear annual observance in the 1st-2nd centuries (McGowan). Absence everywhere not claimed

sources.title: Clement of Alexandria, Stromateis I.21.145-146 (Latin tr. G. Hervet, Basel 1556, UB Basel UBH Rc 8, f.71r)
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 2): Pachon 25 (May 20), Pharmouthi 24/25 (Apr 19/20) etc.; December 25 not listed; not all dates are in spring

sources.title: Chronograph of 354 (Furius Dionysius Filocalus titulavit; dedication to Valentinus), Depositio martyrum: VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae (Mommsen, MGH AA IX = Chronica minora I, 1892, p.71); Strzygowski 1888 Tafel III
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 3): original lost, known through copies; Valentinus as a wealthy Christian is inference; 336 is a reconstructed date from the related bishops list

sources.title: Chronograph of 354, civil calendar, December 25: N INVICTI CM XXX (Graevius, Thesaurus antiquitatum romanarum VIII, Venice 1732, p.102)
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 4): neither solis nor Mithrae is written in the line; December 17 SATVRNALIA

sources.title: Aurelius Victor, De Caesaribus 35.7 (temple of Sol in Rome, 274)
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 5): magnificent shrine of Sol; no explicit source before 354 placing a feast of the sun on December 25 identified

sources.title: Anonymous Syriac marginal note to Dionysius bar Salibi, Vat. sir. 155 f.43v, printed in J. S. Assemani, Bibliotheca Orientalis II (Rome 1721) p.164
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 6): writer and date of the note unknown; pagans celebrated the birthday of the sun on Dec 25, Christians joined, the fathers moved the feast from Jan 6

sources.title: Leo the Great, Sermon 27.4 (mid-5th century)
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 7): people climb the steps of St Peter's, turn and bow to the rising sun; no statement on why the date was chosen

sources.title: Macrobius, Saturnalia I.10.18 (Brescia 1485, Grinnell College)
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 8): seven days; with Dec 17 in the 354 calendar, ends Dec 23

sources.title: S. Hijmans on Mithras and December 25
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 9): no ancient evidence linking Mithras to Dec 25 per the study; a claim about all sources not verified, so narration only says the calendar line does not name him

sources.title: Tertullian, Adversus Iudaeos 8 (ed. Beatus Rhenanus, Basel [1521], ETH Rar 1135, p.115)
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 10): passion on VIII Kalendas Aprilis (March 25); c. 200

sources.title: De solstitiis et aequinoctiis (anonymous, thought to be 4th century); Augustine, De Trinitate IV.5.9 (Basel [1490], UB Basel UBH FJ II 18:2)
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 11): conceived March 25; Augustine: conception believed (creditur) on Mar 25, the day of the passion; birth on Dec 25 by tradition (traditur); early 5th century

sources.title: Epiphanius, Panarion 51.24 (January 6); Armenian Apostolic Church practice
sources.status: Codex 2026-11-20 (research/wom15_原典訳文_20261120.md, check 12): Jan 6 as birth and baptism in the east; the April 6 count is a scholarly reconstruction; Armenian Church celebrates the Nativity on Jan 6 (Jerusalem on Jan 19 civil)

segments.text: Why is Christmas on December twenty-fifth? Every year, on that day, people around the world celebrate the birth of Jesus. And every year, you may hear the same explanation. The early Christians, it is said, simply took over a Roman winter festival, a feast of the sun, or the Saturnalia. It is a tidy answer. But the oldest sources are still here, and they tell a more careful story.

The Gospels describe the birth in Bethlehem, the shepherds, and the star. They never give a day or a month. For about two centuries, we find no clear sign that Christians kept the birthday each year. Around the year two hundred, Clement of Alexandria noted that some people had tried to work out the day. He lists several answers. December twenty-fifth is not among them.

The date first appears in a book made in Rome in the year three fifty-four. It was an illustrated calendar, dedicated to a man named Valentinus, and lettered by the calligrapher Filocalus. The original is lost. We know it through later copies.

One section lists the days on which the church of Rome remembered its martyrs. The very first line reads: eight days before the kalends of January, Christ is born in Bethlehem of Judea. Counted the Roman way, that is December twenty-fifth. Many scholars think this list goes back to about three thirty-six. The same book also has the public Roman calendar. And on the same day, it reads: birthday of the Unconquered, thirty chariot races. The word sun is not written there.
So two celebrations share one date, in one book. Which came first? Scholars have offered two main answers. Let us place the evidence for each, one piece at a time.

The first answer begins with the sun. In two seventy-four, the emperor Aurelian built a magnificent temple in Rome to Sol, the sun god. Perhaps, the idea goes, the church placed the birth of Christ on the sun's own festival. There is support. A note in the margin of a Syriac manuscript says that the pagans celebrated the birthday of the sun on December twenty-fifth, that Christians joined in, and so church leaders moved the feast to that day from January sixth. And in the four hundreds, Pope Leo the Great scolded Christians who climbed the steps of Saint Peter's, then turned around and bowed to the rising sun.

But no one knows who wrote that margin note, or when. It was printed in seventeen twenty-one, and it is not an eyewitness to the choice. Leo, too, does not say why the date was chosen. And no clear source from before three fifty-four has been found that puts a festival of the sun on December twenty-fifth. What about the Saturnalia? The calendar of three fifty-four marks it on December seventeenth, and Macrobius says it lasted seven days. That ends on the twenty-third. You may also hear about the god Mithras. The calendar line does not name him.

The second answer begins not with a birth, but with a death. Early Christian writers tried to work out the day on which Jesus died. Around the year two hundred, Tertullian placed it on March twenty-fifth. Later writers linked that day to the day his life began, the day he was conceived.

A sermon thought to come from the three hundreds says it plainly: our Lord was conceived on March twenty-fifth. Nine months later is December twenty-fifth. Early in the four hundreds, Augustine writes it too. He is believed, Augustine says, to have been conceived on March twenty-fifth, the day on which he also suffered. And he was born, by tradition, on December twenty-fifth.

In the east, many churches kept January sixth as the feast of his birth and baptism. Some scholars think a similar count, from April sixth, lies behind that date, but that is a reconstruction. The Armenian Church still celebrates the birth of Christ on January sixth. And here, too, there is a gap. These writers were working after the feast of December twenty-fifth already existed. Their reasoning may explain how the date was chosen. Or it may be a reason given afterwards.

The Roman date travelled east. In the late three eighties, in the city of Antioch, John Chrysostom told his listeners that they had known this feast for less than ten years. In the west, he said, people had known it from long ago.

So the oldest record is Roman, from the three hundreds. And the two answers are not quite the same kind of evidence. The sun gives us a festival on the same day. The calculation gives us a reason, written by Christians themselves. Neither gives us a record of the choice being made.

There is one more piece. In the first century, Pliny the Elder wrote that the winter solstice falls at about December twenty-fifth, and that the spring equinox seems to fall on March twenty-fifth. These were calendar markers, not exact measurements. But a feast of the sun would fit at the solstice. So would a birth counted nine months from March twenty-fifth. Perhaps the two answers were never really rivals. They may point to the same turning of the year.

So, why is Christmas on December twenty-fifth? The oldest record we have comes from Rome, in the three hundreds. One answer says the date was set beside a festival of the sun. The other says it was counted from March twenty-fifth. Each has evidence, and each has a gap. The sources do not let us choose with certainty.
Every story has an origin. Sometimes, two stories point to the same day.
